proofs.proof_tex:
First fix \(n_B=n_S=n\) and an arbitrary \(R\). For each positive divisor \(k\mid n\), form the equal-square profile with
\[
L=\frac{2n}{k},\qquad a_\ell=b_\ell=k\quad(\ell\in[L]).
\]
The two covering sums are
\[
\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}a_\ell=Lk=2n,
\qquad
\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}b_\ell=Lk=2n.
\]
By the definition of common support, a vector \(z\in\{0,1\}^{L}\) belongs to \(H(a,b)\) exactly when
\[
k\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}z_\ell=n,
\]
the buyer and seller equations being identical. Since \(k\mid n\), this is equivalent to \(\sum_\ell z_\ell=n/k\), and therefore
\[
h(a,b)=\binom{2n/k}{n/k}.
\]
The retention definition gives
\[
F(a,b)=\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}k^2=Lk^2=2nk.
\]
Hence every divisor appearing in the maximum defining \(\Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(R)\) produces a member of \(\mathcal A_{n,n}(R)\) having the same objective value. Maximizing first over that equal-square subfamily and then over the full admissible class proves
\[
\Phi_{n,n}(R)\ge \Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(R).
\]
If the comparator's defining set is empty, its value is \(-\infty\) by definition and the same inequality holds in the extended order.

Now take \(R=4\) and \(n\ge3\). Proposition \texttt{prop:r4-reduction} applies and yields
\[
\Phi_{n,n}(4)=2(n-1)(n-1)+2=2(n-1)^2+2.
\]
For the equal-square comparator, \(k=n\) has
\[
h(a,b)=\binom21=2<4,
\]
so it is infeasible. Every eligible divisor is consequently a proper divisor of \(n\). If \(k\) is a proper positive divisor, then \(n/k\) is an integer at least \(2\), whence
\[
k\le \frac n2
\quad\text{and therefore}\quad
2nk\le n^2.
\]
Taking the maximum over eligible divisors proves \(\Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(4)\le n^2\).

This upper bound is attained exactly for even \(n\). Indeed, if \(n\) is even, \(k=n/2\) is a divisor and its support is
\[
\binom{2n/(n/2)}{n/(n/2)}=\binom42=6\ge4,
\]
so it is eligible and has retention \(2n(n/2)=n^2\). Conversely, equality of the maximum with \(n^2\) requires some eligible divisor \(k\) to satisfy \(2nk=n^2\), hence \(k=n/2\); integrality of this divisor forces \(n\) to be even.

Subtracting the comparator upper bound from the exact full-class value gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
\Phi_{n,n}(4)-\Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(4)
&\ge 2(n-1)^2+2-n^2\\
&=n^2-4n+4=(n-2)^2>0,
\end{aligned}
\]
where the strict inequality uses \(n\ge3\). The ratio is well defined and positive: \(k=1\) is eligible because \(\binom{2n}{n}\ge\binom63=20\ge4\) for \(n\ge3\); the first inequality follows, for example, by iterating
\[
\frac{\binom{2(r+1)}{r+1}}{\binom{2r}{r}}
=\frac{(2r+2)(2r+1)}{(r+1)^2}>1
\qquad(r\ge1).
\]
Division by the positive comparator value and the bound \(\Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(4)\le n^2\) now give
\[
\frac{\Phi_{n,n}(4)}{\Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(4)}
\ge \frac{2(n-1)^2+2}{n^2}
=2-\frac4n+\frac4{n^2}.
\]
Because the numerator is fixed and positive, equality here is equivalent to \(\Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(4)=n^2\), already shown equivalent to evenness of \(n\). The displayed lower bound converges to \(2\); equality along every even \(n\) makes the ratio converge to \(2\) on that subsequence, while the universal lower bound gives limit inferior at least \(2\). Thus the full limit inferior is exactly \(2\).

We first verify that both maxima used below are genuine finite maxima. The catalog \(\mathcal C_R\) is finite by its definition: \(1\le m\le2R\), the positive integer vectors \(u,v\) have totals at most \(2R\), and \(p,q\) range over finite integer intervals. It is nonempty. Set \(t=\lceil R/2\rceil\), take \(m=t\), put \(u_i=v_i=1\) for every \(i\), and take \(p=q=1\). Then
\[
A=D=t\le R\le2R,
\qquad
N_c=\#\{J\subseteq[t]:|J|=1\}=t,
\qquad
2N_c=2t\ge R.
\]
Also \(1\le t\le2R\), so this tuple lies in \(\mathcal C_R\). Theorem \texttt{thm:catalog-feasibility} therefore supplies an admissible profile. Moreover, positivity and the two covering equalities in the definition of \(\mathcal A_{n_B,n_S}(R)\) imply
\[
L\le \min(2n_B,2n_S).
\]
For each such \(L\), there are only finitely many positive integer compositions of the two fixed totals. Thus \(\mathcal A_{n_B,n_S}(R)\) is finite and nonempty, and \(\Phi_{n_B,n_S}(R)\) is attained.

Let \((L,a,b)\) be an optimizer. If \(n_B\le n_S\), Theorem \texttt{thm:optimizer-containment} says that, after one common block permutation, its two large paired blocks and its residual blocks determine a tuple \(c\in\mathcal C_R\), and the profile is the catalog-induced profile \((m+2,a_c,b_c)\). If \(n_S<n_B\), apply the swapped-side clause of the same theorem. A swapped residual tuple \((m,v,u,q,p)\) remains in \(\mathcal C_R\): its two total bounds are interchanged and the defining common-fiber count is unchanged. Swapping its sides back therefore gives a catalog-induced profile in the original orientation. In either case, Theorem \texttt{thm:catalog-feasibility} and the definition of the frontier give
\[
\Phi_{n_B,n_S}(R)
=F(a,b)
=f_c(n_B,n_S)
\le \max_{d\in\mathcal C_R}f_d(n_B,n_S).
\]
Conversely, for every \(d\in\mathcal C_R\), Theorem \texttt{thm:catalog-feasibility} gives
\[
(m_d+2,a_d,b_d)\in\mathcal A_{n_B,n_S}(R)
\quad\text{and}\quad
F(a_d,b_d)=f_d(n_B,n_S).
\]
The defining maximum for \(\Phi_{n_B,n_S}(R)\) consequently satisfies
\[
\max_{d\in\mathcal C_R}f_d(n_B,n_S)
\le \Phi_{n_B,n_S}(R).
\]
Combining the two inequalities proves
\[
\Phi_{n_B,n_S}(R)=\max_{c\in\mathcal C_R}f_c(n_B,n_S).
\]

The same two directions give the asserted equality classification. Every optimizer is carried by containment to a catalog entry whose score equals the frontier, hence to a catalog argmax. Every catalog argmax is admissible by feasibility and has retention equal to the frontier, hence is an optimizer. A permutation of residual coordinates is a common permutation of paired blocks. Exchanging the two large paired blocks replaces
\[
(p,q)\quad\text{by}\quad(A-p,D-q),
\]
and the two displayed large-block sizes in the catalog profile are exchanged. The common-fiber count is preserved by taking set complements, and
\[
pq+(A-p)(D-q)
\]
is preserved by the same simultaneous replacement. Thus simultaneous complementation preserves catalog membership, the induced paired multiset, and its score.

It remains to derive the phase description. For fixed \(c,d\in\mathcal C_R\), the affine-score definition yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
f_c(n_B,n_S)\ge f_d(n_B,n_S)
&\Longleftrightarrow
-D_cn_B-A_cn_S+K_c\ge-D_dn_B-A_dn_S+K_d\\
&\Longleftrightarrow
(D_d-D_c)n_B+(A_d-A_c)n_S\ge K_d-K_c.
\end{aligned}
\]
All coefficients are integers. Since the catalog is finite, the pairwise equality lines form a finite rational affine arrangement. On every relatively open cell of that arrangement the sign of each pairwise score difference is fixed, so the set of catalog maximizers is fixed. On a boundary, retaining the non-strict inequalities above records every tied maximizer. Equivalently, for each nonempty argmax set \(M\subseteq\mathcal C_R\), the locus where the argmax is exactly \(M\) is obtained by imposing equality among entries of \(M\), the displayed non-strict inequalities against all other entries, and strictness precisely off further tie boundaries. These disjoint loci cover the quadrant and give the claimed exact phase partition with all equality cases retained.

proposed_statement_changes.proposed:
For \(n_B=n_S=n\), one has \(\Phi_{n,n}(R)\ge \Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(R)\) for every \(R\). In particular, for \(R=4\) and every \(n\ge3\),
\[
\Phi_{n,n}(4)=2(n-1)^2+2,
\qquad
\Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(4)\le n^2,
\]
and equality in the second display holds if and only if \(n\) is even. Consequently,
\[
\Phi_{n,n}(4)-\Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(4)\ge (n-2)^2>0
\]
and
\[
\frac{\Phi_{n,n}(4)}{\Phi_n^{\mathrm{eq}}(4)}
\ge 2-\frac4n+\frac4{n^2}.
\]
Equality in the ratio bound holds if and only if \(n\) is even. Thus this lower bound tends to \(2\), the actual ratio tends to \(2\) along the even integers, and its limit inferior over all integers \(n\to\infty\) equals \(2\).
proposed_statement_changes.reason: The former isolated numerical witness understated the same-scope consequence of the established exact R=4 reduction. The revised claim proves strict separation for every balanced square of size at least three and records the sharp factor-two lower envelope.

proposed.comparator_claim: Theorem 3.2 establishes validity of Procedure 3.2 for any equal block size \(k\); within that published equal-square family the retained focal count is \(2nk\).
proposed.matched_by: thm:strict-equal-block-delta proves the exact balanced-square \(R=4\) optimum, strict superiority for every \(n\ge3\), and a sharp ratio lower envelope with factor-two limit inferior.

proposed.comparator_claim: The randomization test described in Procedure 1 is valid conditionally at any level.
If \(T\) is imputable, the randomization test is valid at any level \(\alpha\).
Then, \(W\) is uniformly distributed conditional on the event \(\{W\in\mathcal B\}\).
If \(T\) is effect increasing, then \(p^{L+}(D^{\mathrm{obs}},\theta)\) is non-decreasing in \(\theta\).
The concentration probability is maximized when all the \(a_i\) are \(\pm1\).

proposed_core_edits.reason: The Liu--Shaikh--Toulis comparison now records the infinite exact strict separation and its sharp factor-two lower envelope, while all other comparator promises remain unchanged.

prose_updates.tldr: For independently and uniformly half-randomized populations on two unequal market sides, the optimal covering rectangle at required support \(R\) reduces to a finite residual catalog depending only on \(R\). For \(R\ge4\) and \(n_B,n_S\ge4R\), the exact frontier is the maximum of finitely many affine catalog scores and every tie is retained. On balanced squares at \(R=4\), the unrestricted rectangular optimum is exactly \(2(n-1)^2+2\), strictly exceeds the published equal-block optimum for every \(n\ge3\), and has a sharp retention-ratio lower envelope \(2-4/n+4/n^2\) with limit inferior two. A constant-incidence sampler implements the selected event, and null-adjusted focal outcomes yield exact one-sided inversion for a sharp constant total effect. No universal collapse of the catalog to diagonal unit residuals is claimed.

project_justification.gap: The closest exact two-sided-market method proves validity for selected equal blocks and treats block choice within that restricted family; even on balanced square populations it does not optimize over unequal block sizes. General biclique methods establish validity and power guidance but do not classify the optimal covering paired rectangle. Marketplace bias-and-variance analyses motivate the design problem but do not solve this exact rectangle optimization, and existing one-dimensional subset-sum purification does not preserve a prescribed common buyer--seller target fiber.
project_justification.niche: Balanced independent randomization converts admissible covering rectangles into two coupled half-sum profiles. This structure permits an exact finite residual reduction and affine phase analysis for unequal market-side sizes. In the balanced \(R=4\) slice it also yields an exact infinite-family comparison with the published equal-block class, without asserting an unrestricted-biclique optimum.
project_justification.fill: A two-stage concentration argument bounds the residual on the smaller side and uses a support-preserving residual-copy comparison to bound the larger residual. This yields a finite catalog, an exact affine frontier with all catalog ties, and, at \(R=4\), the formula \(2(n-1)^2+2\) versus an equal-block upper bound \(n^2\). The resulting strict gap is at least \((n-2)^2\) and the sharp ratio lower envelope tends to two. The same catalog supports an implementable conditional law and exact one-sided sharp-null inversion. Whether every catalog entry can be purified to a dominating diagonal unit-residual entry remains a separate open question.

prose_updates.related_work: Liu, Shaikh, and Toulis (2026) establish the equal \(k\)-block total-effect test and motivate the support--focal-size trade-off; the present result optimizes over covering paired rectangles through a finite residual catalog and, on every balanced square at \(R=4\), proves exact strict superiority over their equal-block optimum with a sharp factor-two asymptotic lower envelope. Puelz, Basse, Feller, and Toulis (2022) encode imputable tests as bicliques and motivate large bicliques, but do not supply the paired-rectangle classification. Li, Zhao, Johari, and Weintraub (2021) study interference-induced bias and variance in two-sided marketplace experiments, and Johari, Li, Liskovich, and Weintraub (2022) analyze bias under two-sided platform designs; both motivate why focal retention and design choice matter, but neither is a competing exact covering-rectangle optimization result. Basse, Feller, and Toulis (2019) provide the conditioning-mechanism validity theorem used after imputability is verified. Basse, Ding, Feller, and Toulis (2024) provide the orbit-equivariance template, while unequal rectangular profiles require a separate constant-incidence count. Luo, Dasgupta, Xie, and Liu (2021) provide discrete Fisher inversion machinery, specialized here after null-adjusted dyadic imputability and crossing monotonicity are established. Singhal (2019) motivates bilinear subset-sum profiles and one-dimensional purification, but does not furnish a coupled common-fiber-preserving reduction to diagonal unit residuals. Ye et al. (2023) provide the unequal-side marketplace consumer through Platform O's independent user-view and ad randomizations.
prose_updates.interpretation: The finite-catalog result is the actionable design certificate: for fixed resolution \(R\), one enumerates \(\mathcal C_R\), evaluates the affine scores at the two market sizes, and retains every maximizer on a phase boundary. The balanced-square \(R=4\) slice gives a particularly transparent consequence: the optimal rectangular focal count is \(2(n-1)^2+2\), whereas the best published equal-block profile retains at most \(n^2\); equality in that comparator bound occurs exactly for even \(n\). Thus the rectangular-to-equal-block retention ratio is bounded below by \(2-4/n+4/n^2\), attains that bound for even \(n\), and has limit inferior two. The unresolved unit-residual question concerns only whether the already finite computation admits a further universal closed-form collapse; it is not needed for catalog optimality, the infinite strict comparison, sampling, or exact one-sided inversion.
prose_updates.honest_scope: The note proves the finite residual catalog, exact affine frontier and catalog equality cases, the infinite balanced-square \(R=4\) strict separation from the published equal-block class with sharp factor-two limit inferior, the constant-incidence sampler, and exact one-sided inversion under the sharp constant total-effect null. Universal unit-residual purification remains an explicit unresolved question and is not used by those results. The note makes no claim about weak-null validity, power or confidence-width optimality, unrestricted bicliques, minimality of the \(4R\) threshold, ordinary two-sided \(95\)-percent inversion at support \(20\), or the empirical validity of the constant-effect exposure model for Platform O.

statement_notes.justification: An infinite exact separation shows that the catalog is not merely a notational enlargement of the published equal-block family: at every balanced square with support four, unequal blocks strictly improve focal retention, with a sharp factor-two asymptotic lower envelope.
statement_notes.gap: The published equal-square calculation optimizes only over equal block sizes and therefore misses the exact unequal-block optimum even on every balanced square at support four.
statement_notes.consumer: Researchers using the published equal-block rule obtain a certified focal-size improvement for every balanced population size at least three, without changing the underlying independent balanced randomization.

statement_notes.justification: This is the theorem-level kernel: an exact all-resolution value and complete catalog equality classification over unequal margins, with the balanced support-four family giving an explicit strict comparator consequence.
statement_notes.gap: Liu, Shaikh, and Toulis optimize within a chosen equal-block family, while general biclique methods do not provide an explicit structured optimum; marketplace bias-and-variance studies motivate the problem without solving this exact combinatorial frontier.
statement_notes.consumer: A platform can choose the largest focal rectangle attaining a prespecified exact-test resolution before inspecting outcomes.
